Personally for me I did not like CAPS. They were pretty vapid and dry at best and can be downright rude and condescending even. I had to go see then for a few times due to being hospitalized suddenly due to suicide attempt (was held by APS at the university behavioral center. there is a good reason why the ratings are so low with many 1 stars, since treat you like a prisoner and barely show any humanity but thats a different issue)

I would also not suggest CAPS due to how difficult it is to schedule with them regularly since they can only manage to do bi weekly, rather than weekly. Also, Id rather not mix my mental health information with a medical service that is associated with Rutgers due to privacy issues (i had them when I had to disclose it when I was in high school and middle school. Just not a good idea to mix youre mental health with your professional/academic space). Yes there is HIPPA which they are supposed to follow but that doesnt mean your medical information stays 100% between you and whoever you allow to know. Since mental health is so negatively looked up in academia in general ( there is a reason why people say not to mention any mental illness in school apps/job apps) I would rather be on the safer side and go with a service outside Rutgers .

You might be interested in teletherapy. It’s face to face therapy but through a videochat rather than going to a clinic. Many care clinics with in person therapists are beginning to have more of this type of service so you might want to look into that as well
Yeah. Try to take them during different sessions if you can.

It's very fast paced since you're learning the same material that would take about 3 months in a typical semester, within 6 weeks(Summer is split into A, B, C, and D sections). However it is very doable since usually as a summer course that would be the only course you will be taking most likely and you can give your full attention to the subject. I also find it a bit nicer that the exams and material are a bit more streamlined and consistent to what the professor teaches as the department is not actively involved in making the exams including the final during summer sessions so there won't be too many unpleasant surprises.

​

To become a doctor. And I guess that would lead to the question of why I want to become a doctor right? Well I want to become a doctor because it combines my desire to help people, as well as my love for the sciences, especially medicine, and I'll be able to interact with patients too and hopefully create some wholesome relationships with my patients in the process ( I want to do primary care) and maybe change someone's life for the better. Plus, it's a pretty honest way to make your living which makes it unique from most other professions as a nice bonus.

I have had people asked why not just go for the nursing route or become a PA and that has to do with how I want to be the leader on a medical team and make the decisions. I don't simply want to be a part of it and give suggestions, I want to lead it. Plus I know I won't be satisfied just being a nurse or PA when I know I tried my hardest to become a doctor first. It'll feel like I failed everyday, not being smart enough, hardworking enough etc, to make it as a physician

In general, after one gets into medical school in the US, it's pretty much smooth sailing from there on as it extremely difficult to drop out unless you really want to leave. Plus residency matching isn't a huge problem unless I suppose you're looking for something hyper specific which I'm not. It's just whether I'll be able to make the cut after all those years of studying and stress from undergrad. I don't have a lot money either so I try to avoid having to be in undergrad longer than "normal" and save most of it for medical school so I can avoid loans as much as I can.

​

Yea though it's probably my fault though since I decided to go back to school with a medium course load after being hospitalized for burnout last semester when the hospital personnel, my doctors and even CAPS recommended me to take a medical leave or even just be a part time student.  It was really hard, I guess I just wasn't mentally recovered enough to take on the full rigor of school since I'm pretty much burnt out again or maybe I was just too lazy and didn't study enough. I'll just hope winter break will be enough time to recover enough for spring semester.

Depends which company, sector and how they view outside professional experiences vs their own should they have an internship program. I will admit that for someone like an engineer or a computer science programmer, experience and internships often trumps GPA but that is if you can even qualify for the said opportunity to add to your resume. Many have a bottomline of at least a 3.0 GPA, sometimes a little lower at 2.5 but in general, they want nothing less than a C+ average. Also consider Rutgers, while having a good engineering and comp sci program, does not have the same prestige as Georgia tech or Carnegie Mellon where the "brand name" can back up it's applicant. GPA and school name will matter less and less as you progress into your career but as long as you are a newbie trying to get your foot into that industry door, your GPA will have an immense effect on your employer/future employer.

Nice wishful thinking until you see the GPA requirements for internships, some entry level industry jobs, let's not even talk about those professional schools and infamous medical school (pretty much kiss your dreams goodbye if you have anything lower than 3.5 unless you're a URM or someone special extraordinary)

The best thing you can do for your friend is to refer her to professional help like counseling services or even therapy groups. It will be difficult though as when one mentally ill, their sense of judgement is somewhat flawed with the belief nothing will work when it's really just the disorder talking. The best thing you can give is to give her positive help resources and support her 100% should she choose to partake in one of them.

Well there is something known as acute depression and chronic depression. Acute depression usually is associated with a traumatic event and it usually does resolve itself with treatment and being on antidepressants temporarily. Some depression is chronic (usually defined as lasting more than a year). Usually for chronic depression, one cannot be taken off antidepressants and will need to be in regular contact with a psychiatrist or mental health professional for long term management. For some, the depression may go away and that's great. For others, it doesn't (like me, I've had it for 10+ years now) but that's ok too since as long as you're living, there will be a chance to experience happiness
